name: JavaScriptCore (WebKit)
workload: v8-v7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run daily in CI by a third party; JavaScriptCore vs V8 on ubuntu, macOS arm64 and windows.
claimed_speedup: macOS arm64 score 67664 vs V8 64220 (1.05x, derived from page data); RegExp 31307 vs 16440, Richards 52925 vs 47206; V8 is ahead on DeltaBlue (142147 vs 76961) and EarleyBoyer (123391 vs 104765). On ubuntu V8 wins (48107 vs 45928) and on windows V8 wins (46932 vs 41169).
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows runners; CPU models not stated.
tradeoffs: Part of WebKit; engines are prebuilt by the suite's author, so the build configuration is not the project's own.
caveats: Known project: this is extra evidence only. JSC beats V8 only on macOS arm64, by about 5%, and loses on ubuntu and windows; the v8-v7 suite is old and the runner hardware is unnamed. License and last-commit date were not read this session.
found_via: GitHub: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README results tables, found via WebSearch on JavaScript engine benchmarks

name: Bun
language: Rust/TypeScript with the C++ JavaScriptCore engine (repository page language list)
workload: attractivechaos/plb2: nqueen (15 queens), matmul (1500x1500), sudoku (4000 puzzles), bedcov (1M intervals) in plain JavaScript, Bun vs Node with JIT enabled.
claimed_speedup: js:bun+ (Bun 1.0.20) vs js:node+ (Node 21.5.0): nqueen 3.11 s vs 3.73 s; matmul 1.75 s vs 2.88 s (about 1.6x, derived from page data); sudoku 3.07 s vs 3.77 s; bedcov 2.32 s vs 2.45 s. The README text says Bun and Node 'perform well' and are about twice as fast as PyPy.
compiler_and_flags: Bun 1.0.20 and Node 21.5.0 run directly, no flags stated.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (plb2 README; hyperfine timing)
tradeoffs: Different engine (JavaScriptCore rather than V8) with Node-compatible APIs; LGPL-2 statically linked JavaScriptCore per LICENSE.md.
caveats: Evidence for a project already in the catalogue (is_evidence_for_known). Bun 1.0.20 is from late 2023 and Bun has changed since; the margin over Node is small on nqueen, sudoku and bedcov (about 5-19% less time) and only matmul shows a large gap (about 39% less time). Commit date not retrievable (commits page returned no entries).
found_via: attractivechaos/plb2 README table (opened), js:bun+ vs js:node+ rows

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR) fast interpreter vs wasmtime Pulley
workload: CPU time per call on 17 shared interpreter-only cases (fib, sieve, crc32, matmul, convolution, audio DSP, call_indirect, xmrsplayer, vtable dispatch, graphql) with WAMR in fast-interp mode (AOT, JIT and Fast JIT off).
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime: WAMR 1.63 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (WAMR about 1.28x faster, derived from page data); WAMR 1.38 vs Pulley 1.68 on iPhone XS A12 E-cores (about 1.22x faster, derived from page data). Per case on M4: sieve 1.00 vs 1.38, crc32 1.00 vs 1.18, matmul_simd 1.00 vs 1.18, call_indirect 1.58 vs 2.70, xmrsplayer 1.72 vs 2.26. Pulley wins fib_tail (1.00 vs 1.68), relaxed_madd and sqlite3.
compiler_and_flags: WAMR main b70d708d (WAMR-2.4.1-364) plus 29 local patches, cmake Release, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 BULK_MEMORY=1 TAIL_CALL=1 REF_TYPES=1 EXCE_HANDLING=1, WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0); Pulley built with rustc nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS="--cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12", fat LTO, 1 CGU, wasmtime v49.0.0 plus 9 fork commits
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (12 P + 4 E cores), E-cores selected with taskpolicy -b, macOS 27.0; iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores, iOS 18.7.10
tradeoffs: Fast interpreter trades memory and code size for speed; the benchmarked build lacks GC, typed references, memory64, multi-memory and exnref. WAMR needs 29 patches (legacy exception handling, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory) for the Wasm 3.0 feature cases.
caveats: The benchmark repo (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, 3 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-09-26) is third party but its author maintains a patched wasmtime fork, and every runtime is restricted to pure-interpreter mode (no JIT/AOT) for App Store rules, so the baseline is wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not Cranelift-native wasmtime. Numbers are relative CPU time per call (1.00 = fastest runtime on the case), geometric mean over 17 cases that every runtime runs, N=10. WAMR is benchmarked from a patched main snapshot with hardware bounds checks disabled (WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1) and compared with a Pulley fork carrying the author's table-mutability and call_indirect patches. wasm3 is faster than WAMR on most of the same cases (geomean 1.01 vs 1.63 on M4). Evidence for a known project (WAMR already catalogued); reported for the Pulley comparison.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'new WebAssembly runtime github ... benchmark vs wasmtime wasmer wasm3 WAMR coremark startup 2026' surfaced PR #6 of rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark; opened its README and docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md

name: wasm3 vs wasmtime Pulley interpreter
workload: CPU time per call on the 17 shared interpreter-only cases of the wasm-benchmark harness; wasm3 v0.9.0 has no native tier.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime: wasm3 1.01 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 about 2.07x faster, derived from page data); wasm3 1.04 vs Pulley 1.68 on iPhone XS A12 E-cores (about 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Per case on M4: call_indirect 1.00 vs 2.70, xmrsplayer 1.00 vs 2.26, sieve.scalar 1.00 vs 2.85, audio_dsp 1.00 vs 2.35, fib 1.00 vs 1.13. The report states wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 (0cd38327), no patches, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, no WASI sources; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0); Pulley built with rustc nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS="--cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12", fat LTO, 1 CGU, wasmtime v49.0.0 plus 9 fork commits
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (12 P + 4 E cores), E-cores selected with taskpolicy -b, macOS 27.0; iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores, iOS 18.7.10
tradeoffs: wasm3 supports only tail calls and extended-const among the Wasm 3.0 features tested, runs on only some of the cases (no SIMD, no exception handling, no GC), and the maintainer announced a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: The benchmark repo (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, 3 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-09-26) is third party but its author maintains a patched wasmtime fork, and every runtime is restricted to pure-interpreter mode (no JIT/AOT) for App Store rules, so the baseline is wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not Cranelift-native wasmtime. Numbers are relative CPU time per call (1.00 = fastest runtime on the case), geometric mean over 17 cases that every runtime runs, N=10. wasm3 runs only 21 of the 39 cases; the geomean covers the 17 cases that every runtime runs. Instantiation is its weak spot: the extended-const rows cost wasm3 62-122x Pulley's time. Evidence for a known project (wasm3 already catalogued); reported for the Pulley comparison, and wasm3 as measured is an interpreter-only result on Apple Silicon only.

name: WAMR iwasm on the libsodium WebAssembly benchmarks
workload: 70 libsodium primitives (aead, hash, sign, box and others) compiled to WebAssembly, timed in each runtime, December 2022 results.
claimed_speedup: Geomean time ratio over 69 shared benchmarks (derived from page data): iwasm 0.683x of wasmtime (about 1.46x faster), 0.670x of wasmer-cranelift, 0.585x of node (V8); wasmer-llvm 0.872x of wasmtime for comparison.
tradeoffs: WAMR supports interpreter, AOT and JIT modes; AOT needs the separate wamrc compiler and build step.
caveats: Derived by the agent from the raw CSVs in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12/res (libsodium benchmark times, lower is faster; native is 0.289x of wasmtime so lower = faster): geometric mean of per-benchmark time ratios over the 69 benchmarks present in both files. The repo carries no README, hardware, compiler or flag details (Frank Denis's blog posts with the methodology are blocked here), the runtime versions are from December 2022 (the repo was archived 2026-08-19), and the mode in which each runtime ran (for iwasm, interpreter vs wamrc AOT) is not stated in the repo. Evidence for a known project (WAMR already catalogued).

name: wasm2c (WABT) on the libsodium WebAssembly benchmarks
workload: 70 libsodium primitives compiled to WebAssembly then translated to C with wasm2c and built natively, versus the same wasm in each runtime, December 2022 results.
claimed_speedup: Geomean time ratio over 69 shared benchmarks (derived from page data): wasm2c 0.743x of wasmtime (about 1.35x faster), 0.732x of wasmer-cranelift, 0.636x of node (V8).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time translation to C needs a C toolchain and a separate runtime shim (wasm-rt) and gives up dynamic loading.
caveats: Derived by the agent from the raw CSVs in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12/res (libsodium benchmark times, lower is faster; native is 0.289x of wasmtime so lower = faster): geometric mean of per-benchmark time ratios over the 69 benchmarks present in both files. The repo carries no README, hardware, compiler or flag details (Frank Denis's blog posts with the methodology are blocked here), the runtime versions are from December 2022 (the repo was archived 2026-08-19), and the mode in which each runtime ran (for iwasm, interpreter vs wamrc AOT) is not stated in the repo. Evidence for a known project (WABT's wasm2c already catalogued).
